narrative:
The model predicted a 62.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your undergraduate grades in the first and third years of law school, followed by your undergraduate GPA. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest drivers pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class (1 out of 10), far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings strongly signaled to the model that you might struggle with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 actually worked in your favor. It is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Low family income and your LSAT score of 22 (well below the accepted average of 37) also contributed to the rejection, though they carried less weight than your law-school performance.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank in the remaining years, consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score, and explore bar-preparation resources designed for students with similar profiles. Strengthening these areas will directly address the model's main concerns. (248 words)
